item.content:encoded:
Continuing the ongoing series of interviews with creative artists working on various aspects of movie and episodic productions, it is my pleasure to welcome James Laxton. In this interview, he talks about the changes in the industry in the last 15 years, the role of the cinematographer, and his thoughts on generative AI. Between all these and more, James takes a deep dive into his work on the second season of “Beef”.

Kirill: Please tell us about yourself and the path that took you to where you are today.

James: The easy part of that question is that I do have a family member that’s in this industry, and I was introduced not just to movie making and story telling, but also to what goes on under the surface of how these things are made at a quite early age.

My mother is a costume designer of motion picture films, and my childhood was spent oftentimes going to visit her on school holidays. I would fly out to see her wherever she was working in the world, and wander on to a film set, sit there and watch everything – as much as my patience of that age could bear. By no means did I think I wanted to join the industry at that young age, but it was an exposure to a world that not a lot of people knew about.

Then cut to teenage James, around my high school years I started playing with video cameras, making skateboard videos with my teenage friends, and just messing about. It was the advent of videography coming to be more accessible to people, and for me that coupled with an understanding of the larger scope of motion pictures and how they’re made. A few things synergized to me finding interest in filmmaking during my late teens and early twenties.

I went to a film school, and that’s where I got even more narrowed into cinematography in that period of my early twenties. I assisted in live loading film for a long time. I was a second AC for a long time. And during those years I would find weekends or a few weeks at a time to be a cinematographer in my own right. One of those projects did well enough to go to some film festivals. It started to get some attention from other filmmakers of similar ilk, and I started to run with it. It was a longer process than maybe I’m describing, because there’s many years of it not working before it worked – and that’s par for the course for a lot of people in this industry. There’s no fast and easy access point for most people, even for someone who had a parent in the industry. It took ten years or so before it felt like it made sense by any means.


Charles Melton as Austin Davis, Cailee Spaeny as Ashley Miller in episode 201 of “Beef”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: What are the misconceptions or misunderstandings about cinematography that you see from people in your life?

James: The average moviegoer probably might not know anything about the job [laughs]. We all know actors, and we all know writers, and we all know directors – and the general viewing audience probably has an overall sense of what those jobs are. After that, when you look at the credits list, there’s probably a lot of confusion as to what these roles do.

It’s a great job. In many ways, people largely think it has to do with the photography of a project, as the name of the job implies – and that’s not untrue. Of course I’m dealing with the cameras and dealing with lighting on the technical side of things.

Another part of the job that people either don’t know or don’t think about has to do with a lot of creative choices behind those technical choices. That part of the job probably isn’t even taught in film school all that much, to be perfectly honest. There’s a lot of conceptualization and long creative discussions, particularly with the director, but also with the filmmaking group in general. That can get into deep artistic conceptual conversations that have very little to do with what lenses you’re using.

It’s a discipline. At a certain point you need to be able to speak about art history. You need to know some version of film history. You need to be able to understand different cultures and how they communicate. It’s a job that can span a wide spectrum of interests.

The beauty of cinematography is we’re all unique as individuals, and we all come at this from a different perspective. My experience is not someone else’s experience, and therefore I make different creative choices as to where to put the camera, what lighting I might suggest for a certain scene, what colors those lighting choices might emphasize. It’s a great job. I get a lot out of it, and I continue to enjoy it.

Kirill: What would you say are the bigger changes in your part of the world in the last 15-20 years?

James: Like so many industries at this point in 2026, we’re seeing the advent and the impact of AI, and how it can help create ideas and make story-driven choices. Rewind a few years back, and you have the conversations about visual effects around ‘2000s. Between then and now, there’s the advent of digital photography and digital cinematography. The cameras that are coming out are pretty impressive. Rewind further back, and it was different film stocks that were coming out and changing the ability to photograph under different lighting scenarios. These would probably round the top five of the bigger ones.


Carey Mulligan as Lindsay Crane-Martin in episode 201 of “Beef”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: Getting to the show, how did you find your way to it, or perhaps how did it find its way to you?

James: I was a big fan of Season 1 of the show. It was a great season of television, and like so many others, I enjoyed watching it as a general audience member. When I heard that Season 2 was coming up, I put my name in the hat. I didn’t have any insight or access to the people that were involved with making the first season. I didn’t know any of them. I wasn’t friends with them. It was me raising my hand and asking if anybody would be interested in having a conversation with me about it [laughs]. I was lucky that they were.

I had a general meeting with Lee Sung Jin, and from my perspective, within the first 10-15 minutes I felt that there was a real kinship between his perspective of what he was looking for and what I was hoping to give to the project as well. In those conversations I felt that what he was looking for in the cinematographer was something that I was looking for to give.

Kirill: What is the most interesting part of this season for you?

James: I love telling stories about interpersonal, intimate, loving relationships, and that’s what the show is in a very deep way. I love the writing of the show. From the very beginning, I felt it was speaking to so many parts of what the Western human existence is, including the relationships that millennials and Gen Z’s have.

And to speak selfishly about it in terms of the cinematography for a moment, it felt interesting to see that the writing wanted someone who was able to shift between genres within a certain scene. There are moments of laughter, there are moments of tension, there’s some awkwardness, there’s some love, and they all happen at the same moment in many ways. Within the same scene you can effortlessly travel from one tonality to another. It was a challenge that I was interested in accepting. It’s a palette and a canvas that I felt engaged in. It’s a kind of filmmaking that I felt inspired by as a cinematographer.

Kirill: How much time did you spend on the show during all the phases combined?

James: It was about eight months combined on pre-production and production. It’s a bit harder to define for post-production, only because there’s many weeks and months where I’m not involved in it at all, which is the edit process. I do come back at the end when I’m involved in the DI [Digital Intermediate], and that took a few months to get through. We weren’t on it every day, but maybe a couple days a week, chipping away slowly through episodes as they were being turned over by the editing.


Charles Melton as Austin Davis in episode 202 of “Beef”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: One of my favorite parts of the show is the California sunlight. Was the weather cooperating?

James: The weather cooperated very well. It provided us with some classic Southern California sunlight that gave the club those tonalities that we were looking for in terms of our storytelling wants and interests. On the flip side, we had some great gray days as well with stormy clouds. I’m not sure what the assistant director who scheduled the show did to deserve it, but he worked those weather patterns in perfectly. They landed on scenes where we were photographing the Chairwoman Park scenes out of Malibu, and we were hoping for the lack of sun that was in there. I guess you could say we got very lucky in that way.

All the exteriors are naturally lit with sunlight. For continuity reasons, if we lost the sun in terms of our shooting or our scene, and needed to maintain that level of sunlight for a backlight or frontlight, we would bring in our lights to keep that going. If you’re referencing the interiors of the show, and particularly the ones in Joshua’s office and the larger rooms in the club, those are all lit artificially on a soundstage in Los Angeles.

Kirill: Your other major location is Seoul. Did you want to be more corporate there, with those steel blue grays?

James: That’s not untrue. By the time we get to that part of the storytelling in Seoul, we’re looking for a different palette than what we started with in California. Seoul as a city generally, of course, is going to look different than Southern California – and then we wanted to emphasize some different colors that weren’t present in the first few episodes. We were referencing those steel blues and the wintry palette colors for the Chairwoman Park and exteriors in Malibu, and that was aesthetically applied to what we were hoping for in Seoul as well.

Seoul is such a beautiful city, and its palette is so beautiful. It was great to film there. The only thing we did with that footage later in the DI was to emphasize certain things and not to reinvent much else, because it’s such a great place as it was for us.


Charles Melton as Austin Davis, Seoyeon Jang as Eunice in episode 202 of “Beef”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: One of the more memorable sequences for me was the fight sequence in the last episode in the clinic. How much preparation went into that?

James: It’s one of my favorite scenes as well. For those that have seen the show, it’s a fight sequence that is shot as what we call a oner – which is one shot with no edits. As you might imagine, it’s a pretty complicated process to curate. There’s a lot at stake in terms of everyone being in the right place, the choreography of the cast, but then also the choreography of the camera and working with all those positions.

It started in Los Angeles, as he rehearsed and laid out a set on the floor of a soundstage where the cast got a general sense of the kind of space that we’re going to be traveling through would look like. They started working with the stunt team in LA for a few days prior to even flying out to start the process of filming in Seoul. Then when we got there, there was another one or two days of rehearsing the fight sequence at a facility outside of Seoul.

So you have multiple days of that process prior to the shoot day where you rehearse, go through the movements, get more precise, and fine tune some of these choices that were made more broadly otherwise.

It’s a sequence I’m really proud of. It’s quite special. It’s not a random chaotic camera moving through space. We took great pains to make sure that we were going to be in the right moment to see the right reaction from Carey, and spin around to see Charles, or spin around to see Cailee. It might feel random or natural – hopefully – but we were quite painstakingly making sure that what was working for the cast was also going to work for the camera.


Charles Melton as Austin Davis, Cailee Spaeny as Ashley Miller, Carey Mulligan as Lindsay Crane-Martin in episode 208 of “Beef”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: What was the most challenging day, or the most challenging sequence, or the most challenging set to work on – or maybe you already answered with this fight sequence?

James: There’s lots of challenging days, as you might imagine with the television schedule. You’re doing a lot in a condensed amount of time. A lot of our days were hard in terms of how much we needed to make sure we were capturing on any given day. That’s true for our show, much like a lot of other television shows are made in that way as well, of course.

What stands out in particular are the sequences in the clinic in Korea where the couple are separated in different cells by these partitions that are creating silhouettes between them. They can’t see one another, but they’re trying to communicate.

You have one couple who is quite fractured in their relationship at the moment. They are struggling to connect with each other at the time. And each one of them can only see the other through the silhouettes of each other, and there is no bond between them happening. And then you have the other couple where there’s this profile angle of both Oscar and Carey, and those were purposely built to where we could take a window out and photograph them live speaking to one another within the same frame. That was because we wanted to make sure these characters did connect with each other again in a visual way, and not just in terms of the story being told.

We were working with the production design team to make sure these sets were going to be built in a certain way that some of these things were possible for us. We were working with the production design team to make sure the texture of the glass was going to make the silhouette effect happen precisely the way we wanted to do it. Then of course, we’re talking to the cast to make sure that their blocking was going to work with those silhouettes. A lot of different people communicated with each other to make sure each thing was going to work for each discipline, and that took a lot of conversations, planning and effort from everybody.


Oscar Isaac as Josh Martin in episode 208 of “Beef”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: You mentioned earlier that one of the big recent changes, not just in this industry but everywhere, is generative AI. Without asking you to predict how it’s going to look like in the future, what are your thoughts on it today?

James: I’m sure everyone struggles with answering this question because it’s a spectrum. You have people who are fully deep diving into AI image making in a way that, perhaps, reflects their feeling that is the way images will be made forever and ever. And on the other side of the spectrum there are people who are refusing to even touch it. And then there’s everywhere in between.

Today, probably much like any advent of new technology, there are people who embrace it and there are people who are not embracing it. And I think that’s healthy. It’s hard to define what it is today. I hope it’s a time where it gives the storytellers more image-making options than they’d otherwise have. I’m not particularly afraid of it. We should be, of course, turning very lightly and we should be entering this world of AI image-making sure-footedly and not haphazardly, embracing something that might not always be giving us the best results.

I’ve seen a lot of impressive things. I don’t think people should be surprised that someone in my position would say that I’ve yet to be convinced by it. Some of the images I’ve seen from generative AI are quite beautiful, but they’re not something that I would necessarily connect to emotionally in terms of performances and texture. My world exists largely in faces. My job is largely to light spaces, light actors, and capture performances – and the images that I’ve seen so far have yet to give me the sense that it’s something that can deliver emotionally integral storytelling devices in the same way we do today.

Our version of storytelling is, of course, staged. But today, whether it’s film or digital, it’s with people and with light and with sets – whether they’re built on a soundstage or they exist in real life. Those things still evoke an emotion that I feel like I’ve yet to see with generative AI.


Matthew Kim as Woosh, Youn Yuh-jung as Chairwoman Park in episode 206 of “Beef”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: You’ve been in the industry for a while now. What do you feel is the secret or maybe the key ingredients to longevity in this field?

James: The answer to your question is probably already in the question. By definition, it’s perseverance in so many ways.

If you love something, and you enjoy your time, and you feel engaged with filmmaking – or any discipline for that matter – you’re going to keep doing it over and over again until someone tells you that it’s not possible anymore [laughs]. If you care about something that deeply, which I think you need to do if you’re going to enter this industry, it needs to be something that you’re fully engaged with.

If you have the perseverance and you’re going to continue no matter what, at some point it’ll be all right. That can be as short as a few years, or as long as decades if you’re willing to go about doing it. People sometimes break into their careers deep into their middle age, and that’s OK. What’s possible for some people is different for others. If you want it enough and if you keep going, it’ll work out – depends on how you define working out.

Kirill: Two last questions on your favorite things. In a hypothetical scenario where you are on a deserted island, and you can take three movies with you, what would they be?

James: Probably I need to pick some films that I can watch over and over again and not get bored of them, to still have a good time doing it and hopefully keep my spirits up. I don’t want to become a depressive maniac alone on a desert island, so it should be something uplifting.

So the most obvious answers would be some simple ones from my childhood. “Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade”. The first “Jurassic Park”. “E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial” was a great one for me. “Close Encounters of the Third Kind” is another one, and now it’s more than three [laughs] but I can keep on going. Those nostalgic classics would probably be how I would make that choice.

Kirill: What was your favorite dish that you had while you were shooting in Seoul?

James: Of course, you’re going to reference Korean barbecue, which is delicious. For me though, my favorite dish was Dak Juk – rice porridge with chicken, nothing fancy about it. It was so warming and comforting, and it took me back to that childhood comfort food in a way.


Youn Yuh-jung as Chairwoman Park in episode 208 of “Beef”. Courtesy of Netflix.

And here I want to thank James Laxton for taking the time to talk with me about the art and craft of cinematography. I also want to thank Kristy Chan for making this interview happen. The first two seasons of “Beef” are streaming now on Netflix. Finally, if you want to know more about how films and TV shows are made, click here for additional in-depth interviews in this series.

item.content:encoded:
Continuing the ongoing series of interviews with creative artists working on various aspects of movie and episodic productions, it is my pleasure to welcome Julie Schubert. Julie is an Emmy Award winner for her work on “House of Cards”, and later she worked on “Mindhunter”, “Jessica Jones”, “Daredevil”, “Manifest”, and many other productions. In this interview, Julie takes a deep dive into her work on “The Diplomat” for which she just received an Emmy nomination for outstanding casting for a drama series.

Kirill: Please tell us about yourself and the path that took you to where you are today.

Julie: My name is Julie Schubert, and I’m a casting director. I’m based out of New York, but when I work, I work internationally, which is quite exciting. You get to experience a lot of different places and a lot of different people.

I wanted to be an actor ever since I was a kid, and then I went to college and I realized that I was quite bad at it [laughs]. I didn’t know what to do, but I knew that I still wanted to be in the industry in some capacity. My family is in the restaurant business, and as great as that is, that is not a place I wanted to end up. So I got a bunch of internships while I was in college, and one of them happened to be in casting – and that was the best thing for me. You get to work with actors all the time, which I love. You get to work on a lot of different projects in a lot of different worlds, which I love. And you never have to be seen, which I also love.

No one really knew what casting was at that point when I was entering the industry. It didn’t exist in any kind of conversation about what you could do, and you had to almost “happen” upon it. Now it’s a much more prevalent craft, which is fantastic. This year was the first time that casting directors were honored with Oscars for their work, which should have been done a long time ago. BAFTAs are eligible for it, Emmys are eligible for it, and you have these venues where our work is recognized for the craft that it is. There’s also a documentary called “Casting By” that I would highly recommend watching. It gives a great look at the history of it, of what casting is, the subjectivity and the art of casting. Everyone should know what that is.

Kirill: What are the most common misconceptions or misunderstandings about what casting is or isn’t?

Julie: It depends on who you are. There’s a lot of misconception among actors that casting is a gatekeeping profession – that you have to get through us to get jobs. The way I reframe it is that we actually are the best advocates for actors that there possibly could be. We are the ones that are watching what you do on stage and on film. We are having those conversations with our creatives about why you are the perfect person for the roles that we’re currently working on. That’s the biggest one which for me is about reframing that we are your advocates, we are your allies, we are partners in this, and we are not the enemy.


Rufus Sewell as Hal Wyler in episode 302 of “The Diplomat”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: How big of an event was it to see the new category for best achievement in casting to be added to this year’s Oscars?

Julie: It was great to see it joining the other beautiful stages like the BAFTAs and the Emmys. Recognizing the art behind it is hard because it is so subjective – but so is directing, editing or costume design. A lot of those folks who have been recognized for their work wouldn’t be recognized without the cast that they put in front of them that they get to work with.

A lot of what we do is work with those collaborators to help shape what’s on screen, telling the stories that they want to shape, because we know those actors best. We know what they’re capable of, and the kinds of stories that they can tell, and finding a way to make it cohesive and make sense. How many times do you watch something, and you say that was such a great story, but that one actor didn’t feel like they fit into it. Part of casting is to find that seamlessness where you fall into the world and you walk away from it fully believing in it.

You can imagine everyone was so elated seeing this art – that not a lot of people understand – finally getting its due. I learned from incredible casting directors like Juliet Taylor who should have won 15 Oscars already. She’s top of the top. She worked with Mike Nichols and Woody Allen, and her career spans decades. You look at so many movies on all of those lists of must-sees, and she cast them. And without her casts, they wouldn’t be what they are. People are getting their due, and it was exciting to see it.

Kirill: Do you feel that it is more interesting, exciting, challenging for you to be working on an episodic production versus working on a feature film?

Julie: I like them both, and they’re just so very different. Episodic is long-form storytelling, so you get to live in the world for such an incredibly long period of time. But within that come its own unique challenges. You do want to keep it fresh. You want to keep it interesting. You want to make sure that there’s cohesion from day one, episode one of season one, to episode eight of season 20, depending if you’re lucky enough to get that many seasons. And you want to be able to see their trajectory and the arc of it, and be able to follow it and not feel like there’s any misstep. There’s a lot more responsibility in that regard because it is such long-form.

I love the slow pace of film. You take your time. You get to think about every piece in a very specific way. And it’s finite. A lot of times with film you ultimately get your first choice, because you’re not potentially having an actor lose an opportunity later on that may be something that they’re more excited about, or the arc is different, and that’s what they’re sort of leaning in towards.

The thing that I love about “The Diplomat” in particular is because the scripts are so good and the characters are so wonderfully fleshed, we got the first choices that we wanted for each role – which is a little unheard of in the series world.


(L to R) Keri Russell as Kate Wyler, Rufus Sewell as Hal Wyler in episode 305 of “The Diplomat”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: For me as a viewer it feels that episodic productions are now more exciting, and also way more prestigious for actors. Going to your involvement with “House of Cards”, that was the first time I couldn’t believe that I saw all those big name actors on the small screen.

Julie: You’re not wrong, as that definitely set the tone. And we also hit a time where there was so much available that you didn’t know where to look, and things got lost in the sauce. Right now it’s a little leaner. There’s not as much content being filmed. You can pay attention to what’s out there, and let the storytelling do the work of it, and have those actors that you would expect on the big screen to be on those smaller screens. A lot of great writing is in television right now. – and it’s hard to get a movie made.

Kirill: Getting to “The Diplomat”, how did you find your way to it, or maybe how did it find its way to you?

Julie: I interviewed for it. I auditioned for it like actors auditioned for jobs. I read the script, and it was one of the best scripts I’ve read in such a long time. I was desperate to work on it, and I made a complete fool of myself in the meeting. I told Debora Cahn that I would quite literally gnaw off my right arm to work with her on it, and I don’t know why she found that endearing [laughs]. I think I would find it psychotic, but she hired me, and it’s been amazing ever since. I feel so lucky.

Kirill: What is the importance of the first season on a show?

Julie: It’s very important. You’re setting up the world. You are creating the universe that people are going to either love or hate – but you want them to talk about it.

Specifically in “The Diplomat”, you have these interesting characters, and you need to put those pieces together in a way that tells the story – that Debora will be able to use those actors to tell the story, hopefully two, three, four seasons later. The relationships feel authentic. The chemistry is there, and it is cohesive in the way that you need it to be cohesive.

There was a lot of discussion. It was a lot of watching tapes and collaborating with the studio and finding our way forward. I will say that in that initial stage Debora, Janice Williams the producer and I were very much aligned in what our creative vision was for this particular piece. And we’re lucky to have partners in Netflix, and they were supportive of where we wanted to go with it. Then when you went out to the actors, everybody was saying that it was the best thing I’ve read in a long time. Sounds good. Let’s do it. A lot of stars aligned for this one in a great way.


(L to R) Keri Russell as Kate Wyler, Allison Janney as Grace Penn in episode 303 of “The Diplomat”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: How much time are we talking about on the first season? Are we talking about weeks? Are we talking about months of your involvement?

Julie: Months. Generally, when you work on a new series, you get around 10 weeks total to work on that first episode, setting up that world, figuring it out. On “The Diplomat” we had a little extra time. I came on for 3-4 weeks prior to the 10 weeks of casting to figure out who Kate Wyler was. Where were we going to land on Kate Wyler? And also, who was Hal Wyler? What was that pair going to look like? That’s what we circled for 4 weeks as we were figuring out those pieces. Then we took a little break for the holidays, and then we came back in January. And 10 weeks later we had a full cast and we were ready to go.

Kirill: Who are your primary collaborators?

Julie: Showrunners and producers, and especially in the first episode the directors – and also your studio network. Netflix was a really big collaborator as well. What I love about Netflix is that they are so supportive of their creatives. They’re hiring you because they trust you, and they trust your story and your vision. But it is their platform, so it was important for them to be behind it as well.

Kirill: Do you want to hire exceptional individuals or do you want to hire an exceptional ensemble?

Julie: That’s a good question because it’s so specific to each project? I want both. I want all the stars to align and I want everything. It depends on the project. It depends on the team and how much you are all creatively aligned. It happened perfectly on “The Diplomat”. It doesn’t happen on every project that you work on, but for the most part, I’m really proud of the work that I’ve done throughout my career, and there are elements of everything that resonate well.

Kirill: What are your thoughts on typecasting? Sometimes I see an actor, and I say “this guy always plays the bad guys”. Or “this lady always plays the romantic interest”. How difficult is it for you to handle this when you are looking for people to fill particular roles?

Julie: I try really hard not to typecast. What actor wants to play the same role over and over and over and over again? Maybe a couple?

In general, actors do like to stretch, at least the actors that I work with. If you look at my body of work, most of the stuff that I do is character-driven fleshed-out characters. It’s quite rare that I get to do anything that doesn’t have that element to it. So when you have something that is so character-driven, you’re working with actors that are exceptionally skilled in the art of acting. And those actors don’t necessarily want to do the same things over and over. They want to have a diversified career. Because of that I can trust them to work in different places.

I’ve cast Rufus Sewell twice now – in “Kaleidoscope” and then in “The Diplomat”. And what he does in both is very different. He’s so capable, as you can see him in all of these other things that he does where they’re all so interesting. It depends on the role. It depends on the actor. Also in “The Diplomat” you have Rory Kinnear who’s playing the prime minister, and he also played a prime minister in “Black Mirror” in its very first episode.

Kirill: That one was quite difficult to watch.

Julie: Indeed, and it set the tone for that entire series. Going back to it, it’s two very different prime ministers. One part of the conversation with Rory around this question – does he want to do a prime minister again? When you read the material, and you see what’s in front of you, and how it shapes, you couldn’t say no to it, because it was so different. You weren’t going to have those parallels. That’s also part of the conversation – trying not to repeat, because everybody wants something different, everyone wants something unique, and everyone wants something interesting.

It’s the same for Allison Janney and In the same way that we have Allison Janney and Bradley Whitford. Everyone was talking about C.J. and “The West Wing”, but what they’re doing here is so different from what they were doing there. But there is excitement about the idea that you’re getting to have that pairing again.

There’s a lot of different elements to it, but we try really hard not to typecast, if we can.


(L to R) Allison Janney as Grace Penn, Bradley Whitford as Todd Penn in episode 306 of “The Diplomat”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: Is there such a thing as your favorite season on the show, or are they all your babies, so to speak?

Julie: They’re all my babies. But I will say, this is one of those unique shows that I think gets better and better each season. It’s such a rare thing. I loved the first season. And then the second season came out, and it was fantastic. And then the third season came out, and as I was reading the scripts, I couldn’t believe that it’s gotten even better. And now wait till the fourth season, because the fourth season is pretty awesome. It’s so exciting, because it’s getting better and better as it goes.

Kirill: How different is your job today from 20 years ago?

Julie: Very much so. Twenty years ago I was taking VHS tapes, and putting them in two different machines, and trying to record things, and then FedEx’ing them to people in Los Angeles, because all of the creatives lived in Los Angeles at the time. And if you didn’t catch the deadline for FedEx, they wouldn’t get the tape, and your people wouldn’t get cast, and it was terrible.

I don’t think the creative conversations have changed, but the technology has certainly shifted in a way that allows for faster consideration of things, and for actors to have the ability to be wherever they are, whenever they want to be, and still be considered and not lose out on opportunities.

Kirill: I’m not sure how scientifically accurate it is, but I’ve heard a number of times that an average person can hold about 500 names in their memory. How many names do you hold in your head?

Julie: I feel like I have way more than 500. It’s my specialized skill. I don’t know if I could give you an actual count, but if that’s the average, I will exceed the average. That’s my job. I have to remember names. I have to remember faces. I have to remember performances. To be fair though, that also means that I forget a lot of my daily life, because my brain is fully consumed by my job.

Kirill: Do you keep track of everybody’s whereabouts and schedules?

Julie: Yes and no. I read the trades every day, because that gives you an idea of what actors are doing, who’s active, where they are. If I’m working on an international project, I make it a point of knowing where everybody is in that particular market. But I can’t say that I keep up to date with the availability of actors in different parts of the world, unless I’m working on something in those markets. I can always call agents and actors and managers and check their availability if I’m unsure about something.

Kirill: Generative AI is on everybody’s mind lately. How do you see it today for your specific part of the industry and for the industry in general?

Julie: It’s really hard for AI to replace human emotion and human conversation. I know there are going to be certain industries that will be hit hard with it. Right now, I don’t see how casting can be affected by it – unless they want to take the human element out of things.

The reason you hire casting directors is not only for their taste and for their eye, but for their depth of knowledge, and their ability to marry actors with the right roles in a way that the creatives are going to be able to tell the stories that they want to tell. AI can spit out a bunch of names, but they’re not going to tell you why that one is the right role. They’re not going to advocate for that person to get that role.

Going back to “House of Cards”, Rachel Brosnahan was hired for that role that ended up expanding. You put that in AI, it’ll spit out a bunch of names, but it won’t be able to tell you why Rachel was the one that we should have hired. That was me. That was the conversations that I had with the creatives, and the explanation and the body of work and auditions that she put in and all of that work to get her that job.

She’s incredibly talented, and she’d have an amazing career even without that job. But that job gave her the stepping stone to be able to do what she does now – to be in “Superman”, to do “Marvelous Mrs. Maisel”, to do everything that she does, all the advocacy work. It was because someone advocated for her and was passionate about her. That’s what we’re seeing as cast writers do in all aspects of their work, and AI can’t do that. Maybe I’m being optimistic, but that’s what I’m hoping for.


Rory Kinnear as Nicol Trowbridge in episode 102 of “The Diplomat”. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: What do you feel is the secret or the key ingredients to longevity in your part of this industry?

Julie: You really have to have attention to detail. You have to have a real love of actors and knowledge of capability. You have to show up. You have to stand behind your word. And you have to be consistent.

There’s going to be ups and downs in every industry. We’re going to have strikes. There’s going to be an abundance of work, and then there’s going to be a dearth of work. You’re going to have to roll with the punches, and find ways to stay creative, and not burn out and not flame out. Also, it’s helpful to have hobbies outside of this business. This should not be your end-all be-all, the only thing that you have to love.

Kirill: If you had a time machine and you could go back 20 years or so, and give your younger self a piece of advice, what would that be?

Julie: I would say don’t stress out so much. I was a very anxious, very intense person who desperately wanted to prove themselves, and I was always afraid that I wasn’t doing enough. That drive was important to get me where I am today, but it would have been a lot more fun had I just chilled out a little bit.

Kirill: You mentioned that your job took you all over the world. If you had to choose one dish that is your favorite from anywhere in the world, what would it be?

Julie: There was one, around 20 years ago, and I still dream of this dish in San Gimignano in Italy. It was a combination of Italian and Austrian, and it was the best dish I’ve ever had in my entire life. And I can’t find a recipe for it, and it breaks my heart. The fact that I still dream about this dish after 20 years is ridiculous, and I have no idea how to recreate it. It was a fusion, it was savory, there was a pasta element to it, and I would love for you to figure it out and send it to me.


(L to R) Keri Russell as Kate Wyler, Ato Essandoh as Stuart Heyford in episode 103 of “The Diplomat”. Courtesy of Netflix.

And here I want to thank Julie Schubert for taking the time to talk with me about the art and craft of casting. I also want to thank Kristy Chan for making this interview happen. The first three seasons of “The Diplomat” are streaming now on Netflix. Finally, if you want to know more about how films and TV shows are made, click here for additional in-depth interviews in this series.

item.content:encoded:
Continuing the ongoing series of interviews with creative artists working on various aspects of movie and episodic productions, it is my pleasure to welcome Brendan Uegama. In this interview, he talks about the changes in the industry in the last 15 years, the role of the cinematographer, the evolution of tools at his disposal, and his thoughts on generative AI. Between all these and more, Brendan takes a deep dive into his work on the first season of “Star City”.

Kirill: Please tell us about yourself and the path that took you to where you are today.

Brendan: The path that took me here is not a straightforward one, and I think that’s probably true for most people. Going back to high school, I always knew I wanted to make films but I didn’t necessarily think it was possible for quite some time.

At that time my understanding of filmmaking was limited. I didn’t know how many people it took to make a show, what they all did etc. I only really knew about directors and actors. What I did know was that I was always drawn to visual storytelling. I was constantly taking photographs, drawing, and exploring other types of art.

Eventually, I went to film school and studied cinematography full time for a year. I became completely hooked and fell in love with cinema and kept pushing to build my career.

From there, I decided I only wanted to shoot and not work my way through the camera department on set. It was a decision that was right for me however it did mean it took many more years trying to get onto a bigger film set. But like everything you keep pushing and building steps by step. And with some lucky opportunities every now and then I was able to start shooting shows that helped me get to where I am today.

Kirill: Looking at these first 15 or so years in the industry, what are the bigger changes you’ve seen so far?

Brendan: Oh between today and 15 years ago there’s a big shift in filmmaking and in many different areas of the industry. I think the most obvious is the rise of streaming over that time. They are just dominating now. But before them y really had big features, network television and of course independent films. Starting out I was doing independents. It was little projects either on 16mm or on digital, and of course another thing that has drastically changed over that time is digital technology. You can shoot fantastic images on digital cameras now, and we’ve seen huge changes in lighting. You have consoles and LED lights that are fully programmable and that has changed the way that I work more than anything else I think.


Cinematography of “Star City” by Brendan Uegama, courtesy of Apple TV.

Kirill: Would you want to turn back the clock and go back to the old film world?

Brendan: Many parts of me would love that but there’s a lot of good things about both film and digital filmmaking. I do love the process of film, trusting your instincts like that, the workflow on set. But digital allows so much other creativity and freedom. There are pros and cons of both.

It’s pretty unbelievable to look at what we have access to today when it comes to digital cameras. Your main camera can do high speed, be extremely sensitive in low light and small enough to put in configurations that you couldn’t before. And you can get quality images out of cameras the size of smartphones. That kind of flexibility is fantastic.

Kirill: What do you feel are the bigger misunderstandings or misconceptions about the role of the cinematographer?

Brendan: I think one of the biggest misconceptions about the role of the cinematographer is that it’s simply about making things look beautiful. Yes we care a lot about images but the job is really about storytelling and emotion.

A cinematographer is constantly trying to understand what the audience should feel in a moment and then using all the tools we have to support that. Sometimes that means creating something beautiful, and sometimes it means doing the opposite. The most important thing is that the image serves the story.

For me it also means being very involved in as many aspects of production. I want to understand the entire world we are creating so that I can contribute to the storytelling as much as possible. The more I understand the more I can offer the director.


Cinematography of “Star City” by Brendan Uegama, courtesy of Apple TV.

Kirill: Getting to “Star City”, how did it start for you?

Brendan: I was working on a different show with the director Nick Murphy, and one day he came to me on set and told me about his next project, Star City. He said he thought I would be great for it and that he was going to put me forward for it if I was interested.

I read the pilot and I loved it right away as it just hit on so many levels for me. Yes I loved the space exploration element but what really did it was everything beyond that. The espionage, the politics, and most importantly the human side of the story. These were characters living under the immense pressure of an oppressive system, yet they’re still driven by ambition and a belief in something bigger than themselves. They were trying to achieve things they had dreamed about and that they believed could change the world. That universal human struggle was what really resonated with me.

I saw it as much more than a story about space and cosmonauts. It was about people, their sacrifices, their hopes, and what they were willing to endure to achieve something extraordinary.

When I met with the showrunners Matt Wolpert and Ben Nedivi, I was already deeply excited about the project and knew I wanted to be part of it. The lovely thing about this show was that we all came together with a shared passion for the story, the characters, the period, and the desire to tell it in a way that felt truthful and grounded. That made this project incredibly special.

Kirill: How do you maintain consistent visuals with multiple directors and another cinematographer on the same season?

Brendan: So I shot the pilot block and block 3 while Cort Fey shot block 2 and 4. Initially figuring out this show’s approach took months in prep exploring ideas with the whole creative team. There is so much that goes into defining a show’s visual language and everyone involved had the same goal which was to make the best show possible. That commitment goes to anyone who joined the team later.

So to maintain consistency between all directors becomes easy when we are all after the same vision. I just shared as much as I could and explained our ideas for how we came to terms with our visual language.


Cinematography of “Star City” by Brendan Uegama, courtesy of Apple TV.

Kirill: Did you have any particular visual references or inspirations around the discussions on the look of the show?

Brendan: We shot the show in Lithuania starting in February 2025. I found out I was going to be part of the project around September or October 2024, so I’d been thinking about this for a while before starting official prep. During that time I was doing as much research as I could to try and understand that world. Naturally everything started to come together as we started to scout locations.

I did watch some past Soviet films, but my research went more into still photography of the time, around the late 60’s and 70’s. I leaned into photographs that showed me daily life of regular people in the Soviet Union. What people looked like, how they lived, dressed, what the world felt like, what textures I could grab out of there, what the light looked like. When it came time to go to camera there was one thing that we wanted to make sure to do, which was to not have our show feel overly constructed by us filmmakers and more like the scenes were found. We wanted it to feel like we walked into a real space with real people in it, mid conversation and the light was coming from the sources you can see. A lot of this idea was inspired by a lot of this photography.

And of course we built the sets that we wanted and I lit it the way I wanted so that the light felt natural to the space we were in. That’s why my primary inspiration was the photographs of that time rather than the films. Some of the soviet movies that I had watched from that time are so beautifully made but in a different direction than we wanted to go.

I found this photographer named Martin Manhoff who was an American diplomat in Moscow around that time, and he documented a lot with still cameras and movie cameras. His stills and footage opened up a world that I hadn’t seen and it gave me a lot of inspiration for this show.


Cinematography of “Star City” by Brendan Uegama, courtesy of Apple TV.

Kirill: What were your considerations around the colors of the show?

Brendan: I wanted the color of the lighting to be realistic. Whenever possible, I didn’t use LED lights unless needed. Instead, we went for the old incandescent lights and a lot of fluorescents. They both gave either the warmth that felt truthful to the environment and the ugly spiky cast from the fluros that just felt right. For daylight I pushed for cooler tones. The story takes place in winter time, and it was cold in Lithuania, and those winters in Moscow would have been extremely cold as well. I didn’t want to feel any extra warmth in there, so I leaned into that coldness .

For the night exteriors, I lit almost entirely with practical sources. Our art department would provide a bunch of street lights for us and I’d use both sodium and blue-green mercury vapor lights. I loved the mixed color temperatures instead of correcting them which allows them to feel harsher and dirtier and less polished. That visual imperfection became an important part of the show’s atmosphere.


Cinematography of “Star City” by Brendan Uegama, courtesy of Apple TV.

Kirill: You mentioned the oppressing hand of the government that is present throughout the story. What was your thinking around translating that oppression into what we see on screen?

Brendan: Lyudmilla sits at the center of the story, and in many ways she embodies the oppressive nature of the Soviet state. The authoritarian way is felt strongly by most characters living in Star City. We needed to visually express that without calling attention to itself.

We looked for specific moments where the camera could quietly suggest that someone was always watching or that there was an unseen presence just beyond the frame. Whether it was a figure in the background or a subtle point of view, we wanted the audience to feel that surveillance was constant. Because of that we would sometimes let the camera observe from a distance more, allowing the feeling of being watched to become part of the visual language.

So sometimes you’ll see part of a scene happen from more of a distance, or looking at characters through crowds or behind foreground elements, or framing scenes as though we were catching something we weren’t meant to see. Those choices created the sense that an unseen presence could be there or not.

Kirill: What is the split between VFX and in-camera shots?

Brendan: Well my preference is always capturing as much as possible in camera. Star City is a period piece set in a different country, and of course with a fair amount of space work. So yes we had a good amount of VFX.

We would always try to build the shots or sets to look right and complete from the start, and we were lucky to have an amazing production design team that could help us with so much of what was needed to be seen in camera. Whenever we felt we couldn’t go any further with what we could build and photograph, then we would rely on our great VFX team for it.
There is the obvious .. for example the space walk and the surface of the moon that had visual effects. And each shot had to be planned specifically to work seamlessly. But also there are many that don’t seem or look like visual shots that are.

For example, the Security Division building where Lyudmilla and Irina work. The location we used for the lobby area is in Vilnius city, and out the front glass doors you see a busy street with store fronts on the other side. But for us it was supposed to be in the middle of the complex of Star City, which is a secretive area in the middle of the forest. So we put up a large green screen outside the glass doors. We then went to Vingis park and shot some plate shots to comp in as the view.

But like everything it starts from the script. You then start scouting and finding the right locations to tell that story and if they don’t all marry together you sometimes need to cheat them together.


Cinematography of “Star City” by Brendan Uegama, courtesy of Apple TV.

Kirill: What went into the decision to go with anamorphic lenses with soft edges around the image?

Brendan: Lensing is always one of my most essential creative decisions in prep because it informs much more than just the glass. Once I find the right lenses it not only helps me understand how I’m going to photograph the show but also starts defining my visual process for everything.

We prepped out of ARRI Berlin, and I worked closely with Christoph Hoffsten who is a lens guru. I made several trips down there because I knew finding the right lenses was going to define the visual language of the show, so it was very important to test test test. We always knew we wanted to shoot anamorphic. Director Nick Murphy and I are both big fans of the format and we knew we didn’t want a polished overly clean image.

I soon enough figured out I didn’t want one consistent set of lenses. I didn’t want the glass to feel like one unified set. I wanted it to feel like it was pieced together with mixed matched glass that was imperfect in all ways.

So early on I had an idea that I would build a large set out of multiple primes from different manufacturers. I found around eight to ten different manufacturers to make up our lens set, and I gravitated towards lenses that felt like they fell apart in certain areas where the edges were blurrier or they breathed a lot.

Those imperfect qualities that traditionally wouldn’t be considered good quality by today’s lens standards were actually the things I was most drawn to. I wanted those characteristics to become part of the storytelling. They helped create this imperfect, “ugly beautiful” world we were trying to build, and they influenced the emotional feeling of every frame.

Every time I went down to Arri and worked with Christoph, we would spend the day testing numerous lenses. We’d put them on the camera, live with them for a bit, and ask ourselves how they made us feel. The ones that didn’t have the right character went into one pile. The ones that surprised us or had something unique went into another. Over the course of about a month, we slowly assembled this completely hand-picked set of lenses that felt unlike anything you could pull off a shelf.

The lenses themselves informed so much. How we framed scenes, how we photographed faces, how the world felt emotionally. They became a huge part of creating this “ugly beautiful” aesthetic that defined the series.


Cinematography of “Star City” by Brendan Uegama, courtesy of Apple TV.

Kirill: Was there anything particularly complicated or challenging around filming for zero gravity?

Brendan: Zero gravity has a lot of challenges. And it’s a very time consuming thing to do. We came out of it realizing it takes on average a couple hours from rehearsal of a shot to “moving on” to do a proper shot of someone floating through space in any significant way. We have multiple ways of dealing with zero gravity. You have actors on cables suspended from above, you have teeter-totter versions, and then you have your actors faking it a little bit if we’re tight enough.

Every shot had different requirements depending on the relationship between the camera, the actors, and the ship itself. We would storyboard it to know what the shot was, then had to figure out what the best orientation of the ship is best in. Is it upright or on its side or completely upside down? What wall, ceiling or floor panel needed to come out to get the crane in? And if the camera needed to travel from what appears to be the ceiling down to the floor, we might have to flip the entire set so we could achieve that move more naturally.

Every decision affected the physical configuration of the set, the camera, and how the actors would move. Within a single sequence, we might use several different orientations of the ship. That meant we’d often shoot part of the scene one day, then return days later after the construction team had changed the set for us to work better for the next shot.

And of course, making sure the actors knew the shot, felt comfortable with the rig they were in was essential. They needed to feel secure enough that they could hopefully forget about the mechanics of it. So we would first rehearse the action with a stunt performer in the rig so we could work out the movement, timing, and camera approach and the actors could see how it was going to work before they went on the wires. Then we would set up while the actors were being harnessed.

That was the process and every shot required a lot of coordination between performance, safety, camera, lighting, and stunts. It’s what made the work great but also why these sequences were so time consuming.

Kirill: Perhaps you just answered my next question, but I’ll ask it to make sure. What was the most challenging day or sequence or set that you’ve had on this show?

Brendan: Oh that’s a hard one to answer. This isn’t quite the right answer for your question but here’s something that comes to mind. So we had coined this term “ugly beautiful” for us, which really meant embracing imperfections as part of the beauty. The flaws within those imperfections were what made the images feel honest to us.

We built this idea into the photography from the very beginning. Sometimes during the process of shooting, we would find ourselves setting something up and realize that even though the image was nice looking, it wasn’t necessarily right for this world. Those were the moments where we had to challenge ourselves and step away from it, even if what we had created was technically a great image and we would lose time, we would sometimes start over completely because the goal was never just to make something beautiful. It was about making something that felt authentic to this world and stripping away today’s idea of perfect imagery.

Having said that, on a technical level all the space work was the most challenging I think. Perhaps the greatest challenge was the spacewalk that Anastasia does in the first episode along the outside the ship.


Cinematography of “Star City” by Brendan Uegama, courtesy of Apple TV.

Kirill: How do you see the generative AI tools today?

Brendan: It’s a hard question to answer. I’m not an advocate for AI at all. But it’s obviously here to stay and it will impact all aspects of our industry and every industry in the world. For filmmakers, the biggest threat right now is towards VFX artists and performers’ voices I think. But who knows what the future holds for cinematography.

I’m optimistic that audiences are always going to want to watch a project that is made by people with human mistakes in them. Maybe there’s a bump by the camera operator. Maybe the pan over is a beat too late or skies are burnt out, etc. Sometimes those mistakes are what gives a scene that special something. If everything is too perfect, then it’s boring. A lot of shows that are made today are falling into this “perfect” look. But I feel the imperfections are interesting, and we should always look for them and embrace them when they work.

We’ll see what happens in the future with AI, but right now I’m trying to be as optimistic as possible with it, and not think about it too much as being a big destructor for what I do. It hasn’t affected my job yet too much that I can tell [laughs].

At a more general level, if you’re a creative person of any kind, the more that you rely on AI, the worse it’s going to be in the long run. I hope that people try to keep their brain fired all the time and don’t rely on the quick answer that AI always can give you without any thought. Spend a little extra time brainstorming and driving yourself mad trying to figure it out!


Cinematography of “Star City” by Brendan Uegama, courtesy of Apple TV.

Kirill: What piece of advice would you give to your younger self if you could go back in time to around 2010 when you were starting out in the industry?

Brendan: I think the biggest thing is I would tell myself to always trust my gut. Try not to compare my path to others. Don’t listen to the nonsense. Stay inspired. Travel the world. See new cultures, new places and experience new things. Because all of those experiences become part of who you are as a person and therefore as a cinematographer.

Kirill: What would be the three movies that you’d take to a deserted island?

Brendan: If I was on a deserted island I should probably have more uplifting films. But I’d start with these 3 that are anything but that. First would be “Apocalypse Now”. The second is “The Banishment”. And then Kurosawa’s “Ran”.

Kirill: My last question is about your favorite food you had while you were working on this show in Lithuania.

Brendan: There were so many amazing restaurants in Vilnius. I loved the culinary scene. My favorite restaurant by far was an Italian restaurant called Le Travi. A very small menu that changed weekly, a great environment and right near my apartment. I ate there often. But also a standout for me would be a small place that served chebureki, which is not a Lithuanian dish per se – meat seasoned with oregano and other spices, folded with cheese in puff pastry with air inside of it. It was just a simple restaurant but the flavors in this dish were phenomenal.

And here I want to thank Brendan Uegama for taking the time to talk with me about the art and craft of cinematography. I also want to thank Lauren Fein Goldberg for making this interview happen. The first season of “Star City” is streaming now on Apple TV. Finally, if you want to know more about how films and TV shows are made, click here for additional in-depth interviews in this series.
